query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: An ultrathin, conformal Al2O3 coating applied by atomic layer deposition (ALD) on as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will act as an effective oxygen diffusion barrier, significantly improving its oxidation resistance at high temperatures without degrading its intrinsic mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Use a low-temperature ALD process to deposit an ultrathin (few tens of nanometers) Al2O3 coating on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Samples will be exposed in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air) at approximately 1000 °C for up to 100 hours; mechanical tests will be performed under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ at both room temperature and 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent, ultrathin Al2O3 layer that covers the entire surface.
generation.mechanism: The ALD-grown Al2O3 coating acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier that prevents rapid oxidation and associated embrittlement, while its minimal thickness ensures that the core microstructure and thus the mechanical performance (both tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at high temperature) remain unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated samples will exhibit markedly reduced oxygen uptake and oxide scale formation during high-temperature exposure, while maintaining ductility levels of 8–16% at room temperature and a yield strength comparable to 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr shows poor oxygen resistance leading to oxidation-induced embrittlement and degradation of property performance during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is evaluated under a single high-temperature condition (∼1000 °C for up to 100 hours in air) and at specified strain rates (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹); the hypothesis does not yet address potential long-term effects beyond these conditions or cyclic thermal/mechanical loads.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and stability of the ultrathin Al2O3 coating under prolonged or cyclic high-temperature conditions remain to be validated. Additional uncertainty exists regarding potential minor impacts on surface-driven mechanical behaviors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set is ALD-coated with an ultrathin Al2O3 film and the other is left untreated. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, perform identical mechanical tests at room temperature (for tensile ductility) and at 1000 °C (for yield strength) and analyze the surface using microscopy (e.g., TEM or XRD) and weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation.
measurements: Weight gain and oxide scale thickness to assess oxygen uptake
Microstructural analysis (TEM/XRD) of oxide formation and coating integrity
Yield strength at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated samples do not show a significantly reduced rate of oxidation (i.e., comparable weight gains and oxide scale thickness) or if they exhibit a degradation in mechanical properties (tensile ductility or high-temperature yield strength) relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. frame.system: Equiatomic, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy
frame.goal: Achieve enhanced oxygen resistance for high‐temperature service without degrading the alloy's intrinsic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength
frame.limitation: Poor oxygen resistance that leads to oxidation and embrittlement at elevated temperatures, limiting practical high‑temperature use
root_cause_cues: poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use
constraints: only a single intervention is allowed
must not sacrifice the existing useful mechanical performance (8–16% RT tensile ductility, 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C)
relevant to operation at high temperature (around 1000 °C)
applicable at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹
frame.regime: High-temperature exposure at approximately 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air or oxygen-containing environment) over timescales on the order of tens to a hundred hours, with mechanical loading in the specified strain rate range
prior_attempts: Use of the untreated cast alloy, which shows unsatisfactory oxygen resistance
Alloying modifications to improve oxidation performance (implied but not allowed by the ‘single intervention’ constraint) that might compromise mechanical properties
frame.understanding: The hypothesis must design an intervention that forms a robust oxygen diffusion barrier such that the substrate is protected from rapid oxidation while maintaining microstructural integrity and mechanical performance. Prior work on advanced protective coatings (e.g., ALD-grown Al2O3 or other ceramic barrier coatings on refractory alloys) supports that well-adherent, thin oxide or ceramic films can dramatically reduce oxygen ingress. The controlled falsification experiment would involve subjecting both the coated (or otherwise surface-treated) and untreated samples to identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions and mechanical tests, quantifying oxygen uptake, microstructural changes (via microscopy and XRD), and tensile properties. A failure of the intervention would be indicated if the coated sample shows oxidation kinetics and mechanical degradation comparable to the untreated sample.

families.principle: Applying a surface modification or thin-film coating that acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier, thereby preventing rapid oxidation while leaving the bulk properties intact.
cues_for: the goal of forming a robust oxygen diffusion barrier
prior evidence citing advanced protective coatings (e.g., ALD-grown Al2O3) as effective in limiting oxygen ingress
protective coatings can be engineered to be thin and conformal so as not to compromise mechanical performance
cues_against: potential challenges in maintaining coating integrity during mechanical loading, though advanced deposition techniques mitigate this concern
families.best_lever: Utilizing an advanced, low-temperature atomic layer deposition (ALD) process to apply a conformal, ultrathin ceramic (e.g., Al2O3) coating that serves as a robust oxygen barrier under the specified high-temperature and mechanical-loading conditions.

families.principle: Using heat treatments or thermomechanical cycles to foster the formation of a uniform, dense, and adherent protective oxide scale on the surface.
cues_for: yield strength at 1000 °C may benefit from pre-established oxide layers
high-temperature exposure already in the operating regime could allow for controlled oxidation
cues_against: the risk that such treatments might alter the internal microstructure and, thereby, affect ductility or strength
creating a protective film via thermal cycling must be precisely controlled to avoid detrimental scale growth
families.best_lever: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that promotes the formation of a thin, adherent, and dense oxide scale (e.g., forming a native refractory oxide) without altering the bulk properties.

families.principle: Modifying the processing or synthesis method to tailor the as-cast microstructure, possibly affecting diffusion paths or oxide growth kinetics.
cues_against: the current processing route already yields desirable mechanical performance
changing the synthesis route may inadvertently alter the bulk microstructure and compromise ductility or strength
families.best_lever: Implementing a modified casting protocol that subtly refines surface characteristics without altering the bulk microstructure; however, this option appears less targeted than surface treatments.

families.principle: Engineering the internal microstructure (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) to modify diffusion pathways that could influence oxidation kinetics.
cues_for: the existing cast microstructure hints at opportunities to manipulate diffusion through grain boundaries
cues_against: altering microstructure might inadvertently affect ductility and high‐temperature strength
bulk microstructural changes are less direct in their control over oxidation compared to surface barriers
families.best_lever: Refinement of grain boundaries or introducing a gradient microstructure near the surface; however, this approach is less direct and carries risks to the alloy’s mechanical performance.

families.principle: Altering the bulk chemistry to induce formation of more oxidation‐resistant phases—for example, by adding elements which preferentially form protective, adherent oxide scales.

the constraint of a single intervention without sacrificing ductility and high‑temperature strength
